meta.regime: One input is now driving seven of the eight currencies in this file, and it is oil. With Brent at 109.925 and WTI at 98.835 on TradingEconomics, up 10.76% and 9.19% on the month, every central bank that imports energy and has a meeting inside six weeks has repriced hawkish in the space of four sessions: the RBA from 22% to between 41% and 51% for November 3, the RBNZ from 56% to around 80% for October 28, the Bank of Canada from roughly 35% to between 75% and 80% for October 28, and the Fed to about 94% for December. The euro is the one currency that did not join, because its problem is not inflation but credit - the OAT-Bund spread widened to 152.2 basis points even though the French ten-year itself fell 1.5 basis points, since the Bund rallied 5.9, which is money moving within the euro area rather than out of duration generally. The practical consequence is that the dollar is going nowhere despite the most hawkish Fed pricing of the cycle: DXY is 101.775 and plus 0.05%, because a synchronised global repricing cancels out in the crosses and only shows up against the two currencies that have no hawkish story at all, the euro and the yen.

dailyRead: The board turned over today and the agent of the change was a speech, not a data print. Reserve Bank of Australia Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser told a Citi conference in the Asian session that the Australian inflation outlook is materially worse than the Bank forecast in August, that oil prices are running about a third higher than the RBA assumed in those forecasts, that cost pressures are also coming from the AI boom and still-hot demand, and that rate rises are laying pain on top of pain but are necessary to stop inflation expectations becoming entrenched. The market moved immediately: November 3 hike odds, which sat at 22% on Tuesday, are now reported between 40% and 51% depending on the provider, with RateProbability swap-market data at roughly 51% for a move to 4.85%, the ABC at 42% and ActionForex at 40-45%; Goldman Sachs flipped from a hold call to expecting a 25 basis point hike in November. The Australian ten-year rose 4.8 basis points to 5.2790, the largest yield move anywhere in this file, and the Aussie led every cross in the session - AUD/NZD plus 0.32%, AUD/EUR plus 0.30%, AUD/GBP plus 0.25%, AUD/CHF plus 0.21%, AUD/CAD plus 0.14% and AUD/USD plus 0.11% to 0.70100. That is the exact confirmation yesterday's note demanded and did not get. This file demoted the Aussie to the bottom half on Monday with the argument that a currency which cannot gain against a falling dollar has no local bid; today it gained against everything while the dollar was flat, and the leg that broke was the labour-market read, because Hauser explicitly subordinated the September employment fall of 39,329 to the energy and expectations channel. AUD goes to plus 2 and takes the top of the board. The second upgrade is the kiwi, and it corrects a framing error rather than reacting to news. Yesterday this report treated the October 28 RBNZ Monetary Policy Review as close to a non-event and said a soft Q3 CPI would send NZD back toward minus 1. The rate market says the opposite: swaps now price roughly 80-81% for a hike to 3.00% on October 28, up from 56% at the start of the prior week, chief economist Paul Conway has said on the record that the direction for rates is most likely up while calling the October decision wide open, and economists now see fourth-quarter inflation between 4.5% and 4.7% against the Bank's own 3.9% projection, with BNZ expecting the OCR to rise above the RBNZ's published path on elevated oil and a weaker currency. A meeting at 80% does not belong at a score of zero, so NZD moves to plus 1, with conviction held down because tonight's Q3 CPI at 21:45 UTC is the gate and consensus of 0.8% q/q against a 1.5% prior would nearly halve the quarterly pace. Canada keeps plus 2 but the asymmetry has turned against it. The hike is now priced between 75% and 80% for October 28 - Bloomberg swaps at 75% via the Globe and Mail, BBH at 78%, one report at 80% against roughly 35% last Friday - and the trigger was Macklem on October 17 saying the Bank expects to raise its quarterly inflation forecast significantly and quite a bit higher than July, with the risk that inflation broadens and becomes more persistent having gone up; Brent near 110 against the 75 the Bank assumed in July is the whole argument. But two facts cut the other way and both are new. September employment fell 68.3k after a 41.7k fall, a materially worse labour print than the market focused on, and unemployment rose to 6.5%. And the Canadian ten-year fell 6.9 basis points to 3.8930, the largest decline on this board, in the same session the Australian ten-year rose 4.8 - a front-end-up, long-end-down flattening is the curve pricing a policy mistake, not a growth story. BBH calls the 100 basis points of BoC tightening priced over twelve months excessive and Commerzbank calls an October move premature; TradingEconomics own consensus for October 28 is still a hold at 2.25%. CAD stays at plus 2 on the priced probability but the cheap part of that trade is behind us. The euro gets cut again, from minus 1 to minus 2, and the reason is a detail rather than a headline. The French ten-year OAT actually fell 1.5 basis points to 4.9160 today - and the OAT-Bund spread still widened, from 147.8 to 152.2 basis points, because the Bund rallied 5.9 basis points to 3.3936. Money moved into German paper and out of French paper inside the same currency on the same day; that is the fragmentation signature, and it is worse than the parallel selloff this file described yesterday. France also still borrows more dearly than Italy, and the gap grew rather than closed: the OAT at 4.9160 against the BTP at 4.5250 is 39.1 basis points through, up from 36 yesterday. The news flow behind it has not improved - authorities have imposed curfews in several French cities, further demonstrations are planned for Saturday, and the fight is over a 54 billion euro fiscal package containing 43 billion of new measures to pull the deficit down from 5.4% of GDP with negotiations on the 2027 budget raising doubts about the government's capacity to deliver austerity before next year's elections. Set that against an ECB that has told the market it is done: the September accounts said 2.50% already sits within staff estimates of the neutral range, negotiated wage growth has fallen to 2.44% from 2.56% and whole-economy wage growth to 3.0% from 3.4%, and a hold on October 29 is near-universally priced. So the euro is the only currency in this file with a terms-of-trade shock - EU gas 87.92 euros per megawatt hour, plus 3.35% today and plus 19.88% on the month, German gas plus 22.08% - a sovereign-credit problem, and no policy response. It is minus 2 and comfortably last. The yen is downgraded to minus 1, and the trigger is the clearest Hormuz transmission anywhere in this file. Japan posted a September trade deficit of 536.6 billion yen against an expected 181.0 billion, the fifth consecutive monthly deficit, with exports up 16.7% year on year against 20.1% expected and imports up 18.9%; the first half of fiscal 2026 now carries a 2.8 trillion yen deficit, nearly double a year earlier. An economy that imports all its energy is paying a direct tax on Brent at 110, and it is now showing in the trade account rather than only in the forecast. Deputy Governor Himino said this morning that underlying inflation is almost at the 2% target, which is the hawkish counterweight, but the October 30 meeting carries under 5% for a move to 1.50% while December 18 carries about 80%, and Finance Minister Katayama said on Wednesday only that the government is coordinating closely with the Bank. The score is a fundamentals verdict; the tradeable fact is unchanged, because USD/JPY is 158.080 and minus 0.06%, a fifth session inside the same handle, capped by intervention risk at the top and a 223 basis point Treasury-JGB gap at the bottom. Sterling holds plus 1 on a labour market that came in firmer than anyone expected. Unemployment fell to 4.7% from 4.9% in the three months to August, employment rose 102k against 66k, and the employment rate climbed to 75.3%, while total pay decelerated to 3.7% from 3.9% and regular pay ticked up to 3.7% from 3.6%. Megan Greene, one of the three September dissenters, used an LSE speech yesterday to say she continues to believe the Committee should proactively lean against the risk of second-round effects, argued that wage growth is running above the official data and that early-2027 settlements could come in higher, and questioned the Bank's own 3.25% estimate of target-consistent pay growth. November 5 sits between 84% and 89%. None of that changes the structural problem, which is that at this price the data has to confirm rather than improve, and CPI lands inside the hour. The dollar stays at zero and the reason is the most interesting fact on the board. December Fed hike pricing has moved to roughly 94% on CME FedWatch from 75-85% a week ago, driven entirely by oil feeding inflation expectations, with October 28 still an 83% hold and the Committee in blackout; the ten-year is 5.1230 and plus 0.8 basis points. And the dollar has gained nothing for it - DXY is 101.775, plus 0.05% on the day and minus 0.76% on the week. That is the lesson of this session: when every central bank reprices in the same direction at the same time, the move cancels in the crosses, and the way to own the oil-inflation theme is not long dollars but long the commodity currencies whose central banks are furthest behind the curve against the two currencies that have no hawkish story at all. The franc keeps its zero but slipped today - CHF was weaker against every major in the session, CHF/AUD minus 0.35%, CHF/USD minus 0.15%, CHF/JPY minus 0.16%, CHF/CAD minus 0.13% - because a commodity-currency repricing outranks a haven bid on a day with no new escalation. It remains the direct beneficiary of the euro's credit problem, with EUR/CHF minus 0.54% on the week and minus 1.41% on the month and the Swiss ten-year down 1.7 basis points to 0.5110, and the SNB Summary of Monetary Policy Discussions tomorrow at 07:30 UTC is its only scheduled communication before December 10. Commodities stay the engine. The Strait of Hormuz is on day 234 of closure, no fewer than 18 vessels have been targeted in the last fortnight, IMF PortWatch logged four transits on October 18 against a pre-crisis baseline of 85 a day, Houthi strikes hit Saudi energy and transport sites on Monday, and Iran is demanding sanctions relief and an end to the US naval blockade before the waterway reopens. WTI is 98.835 at plus 1.04% and plus 3.94% on the week; Brent is 109.925. Metals are the counter-trade and the signal is unambiguous: gold is 4,115.93 and minus 5.69% on the month, falling through a month in which a major shipping artery was closed, because the December Fed repricing to 94% is lifting real rates faster than the war is lifting haven demand. Silver at 57.310 is minus 14.53% on the month but plus 3.08% on the week, which has compressed the gold-silver ratio to about 71.8 and is the industrial leg decoupling rather than a haven story. Copper is 6.5608 and minus 0.77% on the week after LME stocks rose and the Centinela strike ended, with COMEX inventories at a record 711,609 tons absorbing a Chinese Q3 GDP acceleration to 4.5% and a Yangshan premium at a four-year high of 135 dollars a ton. The cleanest tickets today are the ones with a scored currency at both ends and a catalyst that has already fired: short EUR/AUD and short EUR/CAD at a four-point score gap, long AUD/JPY and long CAD/JPY against a yen paying an energy tax, and long USOIL consistent with the firm loonie. The ones to size down are anything with a UK or New Zealand leg before 22:00 UTC tonight.

USD.when: December 9, now priced at roughly 94% on CME FedWatch against 75-85% a week ago. TradingEconomics has the next decision on October 28 with consensus 4.0%, an 83% hold.
USD.note: TE re-verified the fed funds target range at 3.75-4.00%, upper bound 4.00%, after the September hike delivered unanimously by all 19 policymakers - the first since 2023 - with a majority of the September projections showing one more increase before year-end. The change this week is that the market has stopped treating December as a coin flip: oil feeding inflation expectations took the probability to about 94%, and a Fed statement has been reported as saying most participants assessed that another increase would likely be appropriate by year end. The Committee is in blackout and cannot reprice the near meeting on its own words; the last signal was Chair Warsh at an IMF event in Bangkok on October 16 saying he does not prejudge meetings and repeating that price pressures remain uncomfortably elevated. The data still argues both ways and that is why December rather than October carries the move: September CPI 3.7% headline with 0.6% m/m and 2.6% core, against payrolls of plus 29k from 133k, unemployment up to 4.2% and initial claims of only 199k. Brent near 110 against the 75 the Bank assumed in July is the arithmetic. The Q3 Business Outlook Survey supplies the mechanism: roughly half of firms, up from the previous quarter, plan to pass on cost increases related to the Middle East war and tariffs, and almost a quarter now say it is too hard to say when inflation will return to 2%. catalysts.event: United Kingdom: September CPI y/y (ONS red folder)
catalysts.note: Released above forecast at 3.5% year on year against a 3.4% consensus and 3.1% in August, verified on the ONS bulletin while TradingEconomics still carried the August reading. The detail is more useful than the headline: core CPI matched consensus exactly at 2.8% from 2.6%, CPIH rose to 3.6% from 3.3%, and services inflation accelerated to 3.7% from 3.4%. Transport drove the increase, with motor fuel prices 29.8% higher than a year earlier plus smaller upward effects from air and sea fares, partly offset by hotels rising less than a year ago - so the beat is the oil premium arriving in the UK index rather than fresh domestic pressure, and 3.5% lands on the Bank's own roughly 3.75% fourth-quarter track instead of above it. The asymmetry this report flagged played out exactly: a November 5 hike priced at 84-89% is now effectively locked, and sterling still finished the hour at minus 0.08% on the day, 1.33694. Bailey speaks seven hours later at 13:00 UTC.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: Q3 CPI q/q (Stats NZ red folder)
catalysts.note: The print that validates or destroys the NZD upgrade to plus 1. ForexFactory consensus is 0.8% q/q against a 1.5% prior, which annualises to about 3.8% y/y from 4.1% - a tenth under the RBNZ's own 3.9% projection. The market has moved to roughly 80-81% for an October 28 hike to 3.00% from 56% at the start of the prior week, so this is the last data point before a meeting the Bank's chief economist has publicly called wide open while saying the direction for rates is most likely up. Economists now see Q4 inflation between 4.5% and 4.7% against that 3.9% forecast, and BNZ expects the OCR to rise above the published path on oil and a weaker currency. A print at or under consensus leaves 80% priced into a genuinely open meeting, which is an unstable combination; a print at or above the 1.5% prior makes a third consecutive hike close to certain.

catalysts.event: Canada: September CPI, Median CPI and Trimmed CPI (StatCan red folder)
catalysts.note: ForexFactory consensus was CPI m/m 0.2% from minus 0.1%, Median CPI y/y 2.0% flat and Trimmed CPI y/y 1.9% flat. TradingEconomics re-verified today has headline y/y at 3.1% from 3.0% with core down to 2.2% from 2.4%, Median 2.0% and Trimmed 1.9%. The market ignored the soft cores and traded the expectations channel documented in the Q3 Business Outlook Survey released the same day, and the repricing has held: October 28 now sits between 75% and 80% against roughly 35% on the Friday before. Two days on, the counter-evidence is accumulating rather than fading - September employment fell 68.3k with unemployment at 6.5%, and the Canadian ten-year has given back 6.9 basis points to 3.8930.

Released in the Asian session: a 536.6 billion yen deficit against an expected 181.0 billion, the fifth consecutive monthly shortfall, with exports up 16.7% year on year against 20.1% forecast - a thirteenth straight rise on AI chip demand but a clear deceleration - and imports up 18.9%. The first half of fiscal 2026 now carries a 2.8 trillion yen deficit, nearly double a year earlier. This is the clearest Hormuz transmission in the file and the basis for the JPY downgrade to minus 1: an economy importing all of its energy is paying a direct tax on Brent at 110, and it has now moved from the forecast into the trade account. Analysts noted the sequential narrowing from August's 1.11 trillion owes more to oil disruption than to demand, and expect imports to rebound in October.

catalysts.event: Euro area: Bundesbank President Nagel speaks and the Buba monthly report
catalysts.note: Nagel speaks at 07:15 UTC with the monthly report at 10:00 UTC, eight days before the October 29 ECB decision. The September accounts said the Council saw inflation risks skewed to the upside but stressed not signalling further moves and noted 2.50% already sits within staff estimates of neutral, so the question is whether the Bundesbank accepts that characterisation. More market-relevant would be any comment on the spread: OAT-Bund widened to 152.2 basis points yesterday on a Bund rally rather than a French selloff, which is the fragmentation pattern the ECB least wants to discuss publicly.

catalysts.event: United Kingdom: Bank of England Governor Bailey speaks
catalysts.note: Now the day's live sterling risk, because CPI already cleared. The print beat at 3.5% with services up to 3.7% from 3.4%, but transport and motor fuels at plus 29.8% year on year supplied the overshoot, which is precisely the argument Bailey has used: he has said there is little evidence the energy shock is spreading widely across the economy, and he has favoured holding while conceding that the longer the conflict lasts the harder it will be not to respond. A Governor who repeats the imported-inflation line hours after a fuel-driven beat tells the market that November 5 is an insurance hike rather than the start of a sequence, and with 84-89% already priced for that meeting the only thing left to move is the path beyond it. Greene attacked that framing directly on Monday by claiming wage growth runs above the official data. US crude oil inventories follow at 14:30 UTC.

catalysts.event: Switzerland: SNB Summary of Monetary Policy Discussions
catalysts.note: The only scheduled SNB communication before the December 10 assessment, and the single document that decides whether CHF stays at zero or is upgraded. The franc is drawing euro sovereign flows with EUR/CHF minus 0.54% on the week and minus 1.41% on the month, and the Swiss ten-year at 0.5110 is the lowest yield in this file by a factor of six. The September statement said the Bank remains willing to intervene in foreign exchange markets as necessary; this is where to gauge how close they are to acting on it, and any softening of that language would take every CHF cross in this report with it.

catalysts.event: United States: unemployment claims; Japan national core CPI y/y

Far more important for this board is Japanese national core CPI at 23:30 UTC with a consensus of 2.1% from 1.7%: an acceleration of that size would pull the December 18 Bank of Japan hike forward, break the 158 range in USD/JPY lower, and reverse the JPY downgrade made in this report.

catalysts.note: The first hard read on whether euro-area sovereign stress and the energy shock are reaching activity. catalysts.event: Australia Q3 CPI, RBNZ Monetary Policy Review, Bank of Canada decision with Monetary Policy Report, and the FOMC - all in one day
catalysts.note: The single biggest day of the quarter, and after today's repricings five of this file's eight currencies resolve inside eighteen hours. Australian Q3 CPI at 00:30 UTC is now the gate on a November 3 RBA move priced between 40% and 51% after Hauser called the inflation outlook materially worse, with Goldman, ANZ and Westpac calling a hike against CBA and NAB. The RBNZ Monetary Policy Review carries roughly 80% for a move to 3.00% - a meeting the market treated as a non-event ten days ago. The Bank of Canada at 75-80% publishes a full Monetary Policy Report that Macklem has said will mark the inflation forecast up significantly, against TradingEconomics own consensus of a hold. The FOMC is an 83% hold with December now at roughly 94%. Four hawkish repricings landing on the same day means the cross-rates, not the dollar, are where this resolves.

catalysts.event: ECB Governing Council decision and press conference
catalysts.note: A hold is priced at 82-99% depending on the tracker, with no new staff projections - the next forecast round is December 17, where economists still place the next move. The September accounts are the script: inflation risks skewed to the upside, an explicit preference for not signalling further moves, and the observation that 2.50% already sits within staff estimates of the neutral range. The press conference is where the sovereign-spread question gets asked, with OAT-Bund now at 152.2 basis points and the French ten-year at 4.9160 trading 39.1 basis points through the Italian BTP at 4.5250. Any hint of the fragmentation toolkit would matter far more to the euro than the inflation language, and would be the fastest route to unwinding the minus 2 score.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan decision and Quarterly Outlook Report
catalysts.note: Swaps put a hike to 1.50% at under 5%, with December 18 near 80%, and reporting on October 13 had the Bank leaning against back-to-back moves absent signs that upside inflation risks will increase abruptly. The September decision was 7-2 with Asada and Sato dissenting against the pace of normalisation, so the vote split is the thing to read. Deputy Governor Himino said on October 21 that underlying inflation is almost at the 2% target. The fresh Outlook Report is the more tradeable half, and the fifth consecutive trade deficit gives the Bank a new argument it did not have in September: a weak yen against Brent at 110 is now visibly costing the economy, which is the channel Ueda has used before to justify moving.

catalysts.event: US Treasury refunding announcement, RBA decision, and the US midterm elections
catalysts.note: The RBA decision on November 3 is now a live event rather than a formality: priced between 40% and 51% after Hauser's remarks, two working days after the Q3 CPI that determines it, and with updated RBA forecasts published alongside. The refunding announcement on November 2 matters with the ten-year at 5.1230 after touching 5.36% on October 7, its highest since 2002. The midterms fall the same day as the RBA and five days after the FOMC, which is part of why October was priced at 15-18% while December now carries roughly 94%.

catalysts.event: Bank of England decision with a Monetary Policy Report
catalysts.note: The most heavily priced single meeting on this board at 84-89%, with 54 of 63 economists in the Reuters survey expecting 4% and Barclays, UBS and J.P. Morgan having pulled their calls forward. September was a 6-3 hold with Greene, Mann and Pill preferring an immediate rise, and Greene has since argued the Bank's own 3.25% target-consistent pay estimate is too low and that early-2027 settlements could come in higher. Two things sit between here and there: today's CPI, and the Budget, which lands a week before the meeting and remains the second-order risk nobody is pricing. At this level of conviction sterling's risk is almost entirely to the downside.

catalysts.note: Where the second leg of this cycle currently lives. The Fed's December meeting now carries roughly 94% after moving from 75-85% in a week, which is the largest single change in this file's forward pricing. The RBNZ's December 9 Monetary Policy Statement is its next full forecast round and TradingEconomics carries 3.0% as its own forecast for that date; the Bank of Canada decides the same day. The SNB's December 10 assessment is its only scheduled decision point, with policy at 0% since mid-2025. The ECB on December 17 is the projection meeting where economists place the next euro move. The BoJ on December 18 carries roughly 80% for a hike to 1.50%.

catalysts.event: Strait of Hormuz, the Iranian sanctions-relief demand and the Russian oil sanctions waiver
catalysts.note: Undated, and after today's repricings this is no longer merely the largest risk to the commodity and CAD positions - it is the common input behind the RBA, RBNZ, Bank of Canada and Fed moves at once, which means a de-escalation headline would unwind more of this board in one session than any central bank meeting. The strait is on day 234 of closure. No fewer than 18 vessels have been targeted in the last fortnight, IMF PortWatch logged four transits on October 18 against a pre-crisis baseline of 85 a day, Kpler reports export rates decimated again by Iranian strikes on tankers, and Houthi strikes hit Saudi energy and transport sites on Monday October 19. Iran is demanding sanctions relief and an end to the US naval blockade before the waterway reopens. Against that sits the supply-side offset: the executive order waiving Graham Act sanctions and tariffs on buyers of Russian crude, plus a Treasury waiver letting Russian diesel sales run to April 2027, which is what has kept WTI under 100 while Brent trades 110.

catalysts.event: The French 2027 Budget and the French and Italian street protests
catalysts.note: The driver of the EUR minus 2 score and the thing that would reverse it. Authorities have imposed curfews in several French cities to contain nationwide anti-government protests, with further demonstrations planned for Saturday, and the dispute is over a 54 billion euro fiscal effort including 43 billion in new measures aimed at cutting the deficit from 5.4% of GDP - with negotiations on the 2027 budget raising doubts about the government's capacity to deliver austerity before next year's elections. The market signature is what matters: OAT-Bund widened from 147.8 to 152.2 basis points on a day the OAT itself fell 1.5 basis points to 4.9160, because the Bund rallied 5.9 to 3.3936. That is a flight within the euro area, not a duration move, and France still trades 39.1 basis points through the Italian BTP at 4.5250, wider than yesterday's 36. A clean Budget passage with OAT-Bund compressing back under 120 basis points would take the EUR short, both European index shorts and the EUR/CHF trade away at once.

geopolitics: The Strait of Hormuz has now been closed for 234 days and the market has stopped treating it as a headline risk and started treating it as a permanent change to the inflation outlook - which is the single most important development in this file this week. No fewer than 18 vessels have been targeted in the last fortnight, IMF PortWatch logged four transits on October 18 against a pre-crisis baseline of 85 a day, Kpler reports export rates decimated again by Iranian strikes on tankers in the waterway, and Houthi strikes hit Saudi energy and transport sites on Monday October 19. Iran is demanding sanctions relief and an end to the US naval blockade before the strait reopens. WTI is 98.835 at plus 1.04% on the day, plus 3.94% on the week and plus 9.19% on the month; Brent is 109.925 at plus 10.76% on the month, and the 11.09 dollar spread between them is where the transit risk is actually priced, because Hormuz bites the seaborne grade. The supply-side offset remains the executive order waiving Graham Act sanctions and tariffs on buyers of Russian crude, plus the Treasury waiver letting Russian diesel sales run to April 2027, which is what keeps WTI under the hundred handle while Brent trades 110. The FX transmission has changed character in the last four sessions. Until last week the oil premium was a CAD story and a risk-sentiment story. It is now a monetary-policy story in four currencies simultaneously: Macklem said on October 17 that the Bank of Canada will mark its inflation forecast up significantly because of persistently high crude, taking October 28 from roughly 35% to 75-80%; Hauser said yesterday that oil is about a third higher than the RBA assumed in August and the Australian outlook is materially worse, taking November 3 from 22% to 40-51%; RBNZ chief economist Conway flagged upside risk to the Q4 outlook from fuel prices and a weaker currency, with swaps now at 80% for October 28 against 56% a week earlier; and US December pricing reached roughly 94% from 75-85% on the same input. The two currencies that did not reprice are the ones that cannot. The euro's central bank has said 2.50% already sits within neutral estimates and is absorbing EU gas at 87.92 euros per megawatt hour, plus 19.88% on the month, as a pure terms-of-trade tax on top of a sovereign-credit problem at the French end of its own curve. Japan's central bank is at under 5% for October 30 while the economy posts its fifth consecutive monthly trade deficit, 536.6 billion yen in September against 181.0 billion expected, with the first half of fiscal 2026 running at 2.8 trillion - almost exactly the arithmetic of an energy importer paying 110 dollar Brent. That is why the cleanest tickets in this report pair a commodity currency against the euro or the yen rather than against the dollar: the dollar repriced too, which is why DXY is 101.775 and plus 0.05% on the most hawkish Fed pricing of the cycle. The metals complex is the cross-check and it agrees. Gold is 4,115.93 and minus 5.69% on the month, falling through a month in which a major shipping artery stayed shut, because the December Fed repricing is lifting real rates faster than the conflict is lifting haven demand. A war that makes gold fall is a war the market is pricing as inflationary rather than dangerous, and that read is the single assumption underneath most of the biases in this file. The invalidation is correspondingly concentrated: a credible de-escalation, a reopening of the strait, or an Iranian agreement on sanctions relief would remove the common input behind four separate central-bank repricings at once, and would do more damage to this board in a single session than any scheduled meeting.
